name: American Cancer Society: research, advocacy and screening promotion (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's cancer burden (28% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population), ACS CAN's US policy wins and US screening promotion (72%).
summary: The American Cancer Society funds cancer research ($193m in the year to March 2026: 934 active grants at 219 institutions and its own population and statistics research), campaigns through its advocacy affiliate ACS CAN ($55m: tobacco taxes, insurance coverage of screening and testing, cancer-research budgets), and promotes screening and prevention (about 45% of its $426m patient-support line, a judgment). Research is valued as ACS's share (about 0.25%, drug companies' research included) of the world cancer burden a year of the field's research averts sooner; tobacco advocacy as ACS CAN's share of the US smoking burden a typical year's US tobacco wins avert (the site's shared tobacco figures), coverage advocacy as its share of the US cancer burden the year's coverage and budget wins avert; screening as ACS's share of the year's gain in US screening; the deaths inside every branch's DALYs are valued by age. The result, about 0.006 years of healthy life per $1,000, is low because research results arrive after about 15 years and are shared with a field spending about $70bn a year, policy and screening gains are shared with many groups and fall mostly on people over 50, and a past average counts at the next dollar's share (46%); all three branches are discounted for missing data, since ACS measures no health outcome of its own spending. It is dominated by judgment (the share of the burden the year's policy wins avert, the share of the burden a year of research averts, ACS's shares of the credit), so the result is mostly uncertainty; Hope Lodge, rides to treatment and the helpline are the separate patient-services model.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: smoking DALYs a year, United States (2023)
rows.explainer: The burden ACS CAN's tobacco work (state tax rises, smoke-free and flavour rules) works on: all DALYs GBD attributes to smoking, cancer, heart and lung disease together (shared, facts: tobacco).

rows.label: Share of the burden the advances from one year of the field's research avert each year once in use
rows.explainer: One judgment, the product of how much of the burden the kind of advances funded address and the chance a year's portfolio delivers one (split below for reading). Worked out: US cancer death rates fell 34% from 1991 (ACS impact page), about 1.3% a year and nearer 2% a year in the last decade as lung cancer's targeted drugs and immunotherapy arrived; treatment's part of such falls is about a quarter to a third (colorectal cancer: 12% treatment, 53% screening, 35% risk factors, Edwards et al., Cancer 2010; in the UK smoking's fall gave 51% of the QALYs gained, Glover et al. 2014), and research also produced the screening tests behind much of the rest (smoking's fall is credited to policy, in the advocacy branch, not here), so research-led advances avert about 1.2% of a rich country's burden a year; high-income countries carry about a quarter of the world's cancer DALYs, so about 0.3% of the world burden, plus a lower rate where uptake is low (a quarter of it on three quarters: another 0.2%); about half of that is uptake of older advances rather than the year's new research. So about 0.25%, 0.05% to 0.6%: a little below the British Heart Foundation model's 0.3% for cardiovascular research, whose treatment advances (statins, angioplasty) spread further and faster in poorer countries.

rows.label: Share of that burden the advances from a year of the field's research avert once adopted
rows.explainer: For reading: the share of the burden the kind of advances funded (a targeted drug in its indication, a screening test, a risk factor found) address at the uptake they reach, a few percent each. The result reads only its product with p_success (share_burden_averted_per_research_year), so this split doesn't add a second range.

rows.label: Chance a year's portfolio delivers such an advance (for reading)
rows.explainer: Implied by the two rows above.

rows.label: Years sooner the advance arrives because the field is funded this year
rows.explainer: Without a year of funding, the same advances would come later from the following years' research, industry and other countries; this is how much later. Its credit is split by ACS's share of the field's funding (research_attribution_share_shared), and it already answers 'would it have happened anyway' (Convention 5), so there is no counterfactual adjustment as well. 5 years, as the British Heart Foundation model, checked against the returns-to-research reference class below (ref_dalys_per_gbp against research_dalys_per_gbp_credited); 2 to 15 years.

rows.label: Years from the funding until the result is in practice

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: Calculation of the IRR incorporated an estimated elapsed time of 15 years.

rows.explainer: The lag the UK study of cancer research used between research spending and health gain; cardiovascular research had about 17 years, and screening and guideline work is quicker. Discounted at the shared rate.

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: This produced a best-estimate IRR of 10%, compared with 9% previously estimated for cardiovascular disease research.

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): the sanity bound of references/families/medical-research.md, UK cancer research's return in UK health gains.

rows.label: Reference class: lag (for reading)
rows.explainer: The same lag as the chain.

rows.label: Reference class: value of a QALY in the study (GBP)

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.page: Methods: monetising the QALYs gained (the £25,000 per QALY value, the middle of NICE's threshold range)

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): the study values a QALY at £25,000 (NICE's threshold range) and credits UK research with 17% of UK net monetary benefit.

rows.label: Reference class: UK healthy years per £ of research the return implies (for reading)
rows.explainer: A 10% return with a 15-year lag means each £ buys a stream of about £0.42 of UK health a year from year 15 on; at £25,000 a QALY and the shared discount rate that is about 0.00023 healthy years per £, in the UK alone.

rows.label: The chain's healthy years per £ of ACS research, after evidence and attribution (for reading)
rows.explainer: In GBD-style DALYs, before the deaths are valued by age, so in the reference's units. Against ref_dalys_per_gbp the chain gives about a twelfth. Most of the gap is credit: the reference credits UK public research with 17% of UK gains, several times its share of the world's cancer research funding (the UK is a few percent of it), while the chain credits ACS only its share of all funders including drug companies, whose $50-65bn a year is mostly late-stage trials; the reference also counts the gains from smoking's decline, which the chain gives mostly to policy. We keep the chain, the site's one way for research funders (British Heart Foundation, St. Jude); at the high ends of the research share and ACS's share (industry at half weight) it comes within a factor of three of the reference.

rows.label: Advocacy: people in the United States
rows.explainer: ACS CAN works at federal, state and local level; its coverage and budget wins are spread over the US population (a state's law covers its share of it, which adv_share_burden_averted allows for).

rows.label: Coverage advocacy: cancer DALYs per person a year, United States
rows.explainer: WHO GHE 2023.

rows.label: Coverage advocacy: share of US cancer DALYs the year's coverage and budget wins avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: ACS CAN's coverage and budget wins in a year: biomarker-testing coverage laws in a few more states (23 states had one by March 2026, ACS impact page), coverage of follow-up after an abnormal screening result, and federal budget and coverage protections (cancer-research budgets, Medicaid). Worked out: a few more states' coverage laws reach a few percent of Americans with cancer, and better-targeted treatment or earlier follow-up for some of them cuts their burden by a few percent, about 0.05% of the cancer burden. 0.05%, 0.01% to 0.2%. Its tobacco wins are the tobacco branch (tob_).

rows.label: Coverage advocacy: years from the policy taking effect until the health gain
rows.explainer: Counted from when the policy takes effect (the wait before that is adv_years_until_effect, so no year is discounted twice). Coverage of screening follow-up and of biomarker testing acts through diagnoses and treatment within a few years. 3 years, 1 to 6. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted per person per year of the wins in effect
rows.explainer: The US cancer burden per person times the share the wins avert, discounted for the wait until the health gain.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of a typical year's wins that a year's work produces
rows.explainer: 1: the branch counts a typical year's wins against a year's spending (a past average). Each campaign runs two to three years, so a year's work buys part of this year's wins and part of the next years'; in the steady state that is one year's worth of wins, as in charityevals' Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids model. The chance that the work made a difference is the credit share and the years a win counts ($win_years_counted).

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won policy counts
rows.explainer: The site's one number of years a won reform brings forward (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: No study measures this lag, so there is no reference class beyond the laws' own dates: coverage laws usually take effect on a set date after passing and budget decisions with the fiscal year they fund, so within a year (half a year to two for those phased in).

rows.label: Advocacy: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: At the shared rate.

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted by the year's wins (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The template's advocacy chain.

rows.label: Advocacy: value of a cancer death at 70 or older (United States, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70-74 and 75-79 (their mean) and for 80 and over (80-84; 85 and over has the same weight), mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older (WHO GHE 2023).

rows.label: Advocacy: value of a cancer death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of cancer deaths (in the United States, WHO GHE 2023, facts: death_ages), 50-69 at the 50-74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights, times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Advocacy: deaths per cancer DALY (United States)
rows.explainer: Turns the branch's DALYs back into deaths, each valued by age.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of cancer DALYs that are illness (United States)
rows.explainer: Kept as DALYs.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: share of US smoking DALYs a typical year's US tobacco-control wins avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: tobacco) for the wins of everyone working on US tobacco control in a year: one or two state tax rises, local flavour bans, youth rules and court wins. 0.25%, worked out from a price elasticity of about -0.4, half of it fewer smokers. ACS CAN's part of the credit is tob_attribution_share_shared.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: discount for the wait from the policy to the health gain
rows.explainer: About half of a tobacco policy's long-run cut in smoking comes from smokers quitting, whose gain comes about 8 years later, the rest from young people who never start, about 40 years later (shared figures, facts: tobacco), each discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: share of a typical year's wins that a year's work produces
rows.explainer: 1, as for coverage (adv_p_success): a typical year's wins against a year's spending, in the steady state.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: tobacco): taxes at once or at the next budget year, regulations within months to two years.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted) and the wait until it takes effect, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: DALYs averted by a typical year's US tobacco wins (all groups', before credit)
Tobacco advocacy: value of a smoking death at 70 or older (United States, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70-74 and 75-79 (their mean) and for 80 and over, mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: value of a smoking death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of US smoking deaths (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: smoking deaths per smoking DALY (United States)
rows.explainer: GBD 2023 (facts: death_ages): turns the DALYs back into the deaths behind them.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: share of smoking DALYs that are illness
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (facts: death_ages): mostly chronic lung disease; kept as DALYs.

rows.label: Screening: share of US cancer DALYs from cancers with recommended screening
rows.explainer: Lung, colorectal, breast and cervical cancer are about 41% of US cancer DALYs (WHO GHE 2023), lung alone about a fifth: 41% if all lung cancer were screenable, but only long-term heavy smokers are eligible for lung screening. 30%, 20% to 41%.

rows.label: Screening: US cancer DALYs from screenable cancers
rows.explainer: The burden screening can reach.

rows.label: Screening: gain in the share of eligible Americans up to date with screening in a year, from all promotion
rows.explainer: US colorectal screening among 50-75-year-olds rose from about 54% in 2002 to about 72% by 2021, about 1 point a year, with ACS's National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable, CDC's programme and health systems pushing it; breast and cervical coverage are flat and lung screening rose from a few percent to about 16% of those eligible. About 0.8 points a year across the screenable cancers, 0.3 to 1.5 points; the part due to promotion rather than insurance and habit is in screen_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Screening: cut in cancer deaths among people brought up to date with screening

source.title: Lin et al. (2021), Screening for Colorectal Cancer: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force, JAMA 325:1978
source.quote: was associated with a decrease in CRC-specific mortality (incidence rate ratio, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.68-0.80])
source.note: Abstract (Europe PMC record of PMID 34003220): one- or two-time flexible sigmoidoscopy against no screening in randomized trials. Mammography's and low-dose CT's trials show about 20% fewer deaths from the cancer; cervical screening's effect is larger.

rows.explainer: The trials' effect on deaths from the screened cancer among those invited (about a quarter fewer), a little more among those actually screened: 25%, 15% to 40%.

rows.label: Screening: years a gain in coverage counts
rows.explainer: People brought up to date stay screened for a test interval (a year for stool tests and mammograms, ten for colonoscopy), and many keep the habit; we count three years of the higher coverage, 1 to 6, as the coverage gain is a yearly flow.

rows.label: Screening: years from screening until the deaths averted
rows.explainer: Screening trials show mortality falling from about 5 years after the screening and for a decade or more (sigmoidoscopy, mammography). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Screening: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: At the shared rate.

rows.label: Screening: DALYs averted by the year's gain in screening (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The screenable burden among the people newly up to date (their share of the eligible population times the burden) times the cut in deaths, for the years counted.

rows.label: Screening: value of a cancer death at 70 or older (United States, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70-74 and 75-79 (their mean) and for 80 and over (80-84; 85 and over has the same weight), mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older (WHO GHE 2023).

rows.label: Screening: value of a cancer death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of cancer deaths (in the United States, WHO GHE 2023, facts: death_ages), 50-69 at the 50-74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights, times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Screening: deaths per cancer DALY (United States)
rows.explainer: As advocacy.

rows.label: Screening: share of cancer DALYs that are illness (United States)
rows.explainer: As advocacy.

rows.label: Research: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The research chain rests on judgments calibrated to returns-to-research studies, which their authors call best-case estimates. 0.7, as the British Heart Foundation model; the range runs to face value.

rows.label: Research: ACS's share of the world's cancer research funding
rows.explainer: The years brought forward are the whole field's, so ACS is credited with its share of all funders' spending on it ($193m of research a year). Anchors: public and philanthropic cancer research awards worldwide totalled $51.4bn over 2016-2023, about $6.4bn a year (Head et al., Lancet Oncology 2025, via Euronews), an undercount next to the US National Cancer Institute's own budget of about $7bn a year, so non-commercial funding is about $10-15bn; drug companies sold $252bn of cancer medicines in 2024 (IQVIA Institute, Global Oncology Trends 2024) and spend about a fifth to a quarter of sales on research and development, so about $50-65bn a year on oncology. Industry counted in full, as for the British Heart Foundation: ACS is about 0.25% of roughly $65-80bn. The range runs from a larger industry total ($80bn of R&D and more non-commercial funding, 0.12%) to industry at half weight (0.6%).

rows.label: Advocacy: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Coverage laws' effects on use of testing and follow-up are less well measured than tobacco taxes' (the tobacco branch reads the shared 0.8); the step from use to deaths averted is the screening branch's. 0.6, as the screening branch.

rows.label: Coverage advocacy: ACS CAN's share of the people and money behind the wins
rows.explainer: Coverage and budget campaigns are coalitions: patient groups (the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society, Susan G. Komen), the American Heart Association, medical societies, health departments, legislators' staff. ACS CAN has staff and volunteers in every state and is often the largest member; 30%, 15% to 50%.

rows.label: Screening: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The mortality effect is from trials, but people brought into screening by promotion may be at lower risk than trial participants and complete follow-up less often (a positive stool test not followed by colonoscopy). 0.6, 0.35 to 0.9.

rows.label: Screening: share of the coverage gain due to promotion rather than insurance changes and habit
rows.explainer: The reference class is trials of screening promotion: the Community Preventive Services Task Force's review of multicomponent interventions (reminders, outreach, fewer barriers) found a median rise of 15.4 percentage points in colorectal screening among the people reached. No study splits the national rise in coverage between promotion and its other causes (the Affordable Care Act's free preventive care, Medicaid expansion, stool tests by mail). Promotion explains part: half, a quarter to three quarters.

rows.label: Screening: ACS's share of the resources behind the promotion
rows.explainer: CDC's screening programmes, health systems' own outreach, insurers and other charities do most of it; ACS convenes the colorectal, lung and breast roundtables, writes screening guidelines (it lowered the colorectal starting age to 45 in 2018, three years before the Task Force) and runs partnerships with community health centres. 15%, 5% to 30%.

rows.label: Research: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: ACS measures no health outcome of its own spending in this branch; the chain is built from the research on this kind of work (Convention 12).

rows.label: Advocacy: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: ACS measures no health outcome of its own spending in this branch; the chain is built from the research on this kind of work (Convention 12).

rows.label: Screening: discount for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: ACS measures no health outcome of its own spending in this branch; the chain is built from the research on this kind of work (Convention 12).

rows.label: Research: counterfactual
rows.explainer: Answered by years_brought_forward (Convention 5).

rows.label: Advocacy: counterfactual
rows.explainer: Answered by adv_p_success and the years a win counts ($win_years_counted brings it forward that long).

rows.label: research: attribution share
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources behind the outcome (Convention 2).

rows.label: adv: attribution share
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources behind the outcome (Convention 2).

rows.label: screen: attribution share
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources behind the outcome (Convention 2).

rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: research: illness averted, credited (DALYs)
rows.explainer: The illness part of the branch's DALYs, after its adjustments.

rows.label: research: deaths averted, valued by age, credited (units of value)
rows.explainer: The deaths inside the branch's DALYs, valued by age, after its adjustments.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The shared figure for US tobacco wins (facts: tobacco): price elasticities and flavour-restriction studies are well established; the step to less burden in the steady state less so. 0.8.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: share of the wins enforced as written
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: tobacco): taxes are collected and age and flavour rules mostly enforced; illegal e-cigarettes and cross-border buying leak some. 0.9.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: ACS CAN's share of the people and money behind the wins
rows.explainer: US tobacco wins are coalition wins: the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids (12% in its own model), the American Heart Association, the American Lung Association, Truth Initiative, state and local health departments and coalitions, legislators' staff. ACS CAN has staff and volunteers in every state and is often the largest member; 30%, 15% to 50%.

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: no change in smoking from ACS CAN's own wins is measured; the share averted is our judgment from price elasticities (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: answered by the years a win counts ($win_years_counted) (Convention 5).

rows.label: Tobacco advocacy: ACS CAN's share of the credit
Tobacco advocacy: product of adjustments
Tobacco advocacy side effect: second-hand smoke averted, as a share of the smoking burden averted
rows.explainer: Fewer smokers means less second-hand smoke for the people around them, which GBD counts apart from smoking (US 2023: 1.0 million DALYs against 9.4 million, 10%, facts: tobacco); smoke-free laws cut it directly. Taken as falling in step with smoking and valued with the smokers' ages.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits not counted: ACS's cancer statistics (Cancer Facts & Figures, used by health departments and researchers everywhere), the research workforce it trains (665 trainees), HPV-vaccination promotion and the public education inside the screening branch's cost. Harms: overdiagnosis and false positives from more screening (a few percent of the deaths averted in mammography and lung-screening trials' balance sheets), research effort drawn from other diseases. Slightly positive: 5%, -10% to 20%.
